newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore heading for asset deflation - Schroders.
newsitem.headline: Singapore heading for asset deflation - Schroders.

text.p: Singapore is heading for a period of asset deflation after a property boom pushed home prices up by more than 100 percent in 1993-1995, Kevin Scully, managing director of Schroders Securities Singapore, said in his October strategy note.
The increasing signs of asset deflation "will dampen domestic consumption and subdue the recovery in external demand from the eventual pick-up in electronics," he said.
Scroders has revised its gross domestic product (GDP) growth projections for 1996 and 1997 to 6.3 percent and 5.5 percent respectively, from 7.1 percent and 6.3 percent.
"The deflation is linked to the sudden and sharp increase in personal leverage which will peak some time in 1998," he said.
He expects households are likely to see almost 60 percent of their income being diverted to pay leveraged property debt.
The trend would have a dampening effect on consumption levels and the earnings of banks, property and consumer durable companies.

"With these sectors forming a significant part of Singapore's market capitalisation, we would continue to underweight the Singapore market as share prices have not yet reflected the slower earnings outlook."

Scully said the Monetary Authority of Singapore had already highlighted in August 1996 that the high leverage of individuals will dampen consumption for the next few years. This is in spite of expected growth in total income.
"Consumption expenditure is likely to be weak and this will have an impact on sustainable GDP growth as more than 50 percent of GDP is driven by private consumption," Scully said.

Schroders expects the deflation would take two percent off GDP growth in the short term, which would keep GDP growth below seven percent for the next few years even if external demand for electronics, a key sector for Singapore exports, improves.

"There is very little that the government can do in the short term to degear private individuals other than to ensure that they still have jobs and that annual wage growth is reasonable," the strategy note added.
